first.text: An old man in a sacking smock is raking turf over a smoking vent. He doesn't look up until your ember's light is on his hands. Then he looks at it for a long while.
You're not the Lamp. Lamp's taller. Lamp's... You're not the Lamp.
Hob. Hob Marl. This is my clamp. Was. Is. Somebody has to keep it in, or it burns through to ash, and ash is no good to anybody.
You came up the lanterns? Good. Good. Don't go up the road. The road goes where it likes. The road goes where the lanterns are, when there are lanterns.

greet.text: Bottom of the road. Bottom of the road. Somebody's got to be at it, and it's me.
Daylight. Proper daylight, on the road. I'd forgotten the colour of it.
Light's up on the ridge. See it? The road's a road again. Bram Kettle's waiting on me, I said I'd come in.
Up the lanterns again. Good. Good.
Salt-bringer. Mind the vents, they're hot on the windward side.
Ottie's home. Ottie Swale's on his seat. Came down the lanterns in the dark like he'd never been gone.
In his boots. Told him he'd want them. Told him.
In sacking. You've got his boots. Give a man his boots.
One. That's one. Three to come.
Ottie came down past my mark. Past me, in the dark, and stopped, and said my name. I crossed him through on the stick. Three to go.
There's a man on the seat by the cold hut. Charcoal man, by his hands. Talks to me like he's known me years. Nice enough. It's always been just me this side of the ridge. Hasn't it?
Four. Four home. Ottie on his seat, and Wenna and the Drays came down the lanterns with lights of their own, and said my name, all three.
Ottie brought a lantern for my hut. Said he'd promised. He had, too. Years back. I'd forgotten. He hadn't.
I've stopped counting. Stopped. Don't know what to do with my hands.
They came down past my mark. Three, behind Ottie's light, and stopped one at a time, and said their names. I crossed them through. All four. Nothing left on the stick to cross.
Somebody's to be at the bottom of a road. Doesn't have to be counting, now. Can just be sitting.

There's more charcoal folk in the clearing now. Four. Came down off the ridge in the night with Keeper's lanterns. Talk to me like they've known me years. One brought a lantern for my hut. Said he'd promised. Nice of him. I don't mind it. I don't mind it at all.
Fourth mark's dark. Dark. Somebody's had the lantern off it. I'll walk it blind. I've walked it blind before. Have I?
Fourth mark's dark and there's a light on the stair. Lamp's moved it. Lamp's never moved one. I'll walk the fourth blind. I can. I can.

choice.text: Who hangs the lanterns?
Do you bring the sacks down to the jetty?
The fog stays out of your clearing.
Where are the other charcoal folk?
A kid at the camp found a tally stick by your sacks.
Bram Kettle sends your salt.
I've been up on the ridge. I met the Lamp.
This cap hung on the waymark at the foot of the stair.
Who lived in the cold hut?
Ottie's boots. I didn't burn them. Here.
The Ridge Light wants something remembered. Something Thornwold can spare.
You keep looking up at the ridge.
Goodbye.

lamp.text: The Lamp. Comes along the ridge at dusk with a lantern going, and next morning there's a lantern on a waymark that hadn't one. Keeper's way, that: lights on the road.
Never seen a face. Never asked. You don't ask the Lamp. You don't... The Lamp's light is like yours. Proper light. The grey stands off it.
He points his rake north, past the clearing, at the black line of the ridge above the trees. Up there, very small, a lantern burns on a waymark nobody could reach from here.
Beacon's up there. Top of the road. The Lamp lives by it, I'd say. I'd say, if I knew.

sacks.text: Every few nights. Load the cart, wait for dark, pull it down the lanterns to the brambles. The brambles let the cart by. They know me. You lift the canes and say who you are.
Leave the sacks by the water, take the salt, come home. That's the trade. Always was.
He stops. He looks at his hands, black to the elbow.
Take the salt. Did I take the salt? I'd remember salt. There's none in the hut. I'd... There's none in the hut.
Salt's in the hut now. Bram Kettle's salt. I've put it on the shelf by the door, where I'll see it going out.

clearing.text: The woods like us. Always have. We burn what they drop, never what they grow, and they keep the grey off our fires.
The fog stands at the edge of the clearing, close as a held breath, and comes no further, as if it had been asked not to.

others.text: Five hearths, this side of the ridge. Five clamps going. Now there's mine.
They went up after the Lamp, one at a time, to ask for a lantern of their own. Or they went home. I'd know if they'd gone home. I'd...
He looks across the clearing at the second hut. Its hearth is cold, and a rake leans by its door where somebody meant to come back for it.

stick.text: Half a notch at the end? Ash-wood, with a hole for a thong?
That's mine. That's my count. That's the night I forgot what I was counting. Stopped with the knife in the wood.
Let the kid keep it. I've started a new one. It's shorter.

salt.text: You hold out the crock. He lifts the lid, licks a black thumb, dips it and tastes.
Something comes back into his face, slowly, the way colour comes back into a coal you blow on.
Bram Kettle. Big lad. Mother was Saltmarrow. He keeps a board. He'll want it on his board.
Tell him Hob Marl had his salt. Tell him... tell him I'll come in by daylight. When the road's a road again.

met_lamp.text: Up the... You stood the ladder? It's been down since... since.
You saw the face? No. No. Nobody does. You don't ask the Lamp.
You think of the four who went up asking for a lantern, and of the ladder put down so there'd be no fifth, and you look at the old man raking his clamp, and you don't say it.

cap.text: He takes the cap in both black hands and turns it over, and finds the cord sewn round the band with his thumb.
Ottie's. Ottie Swale. Sewed that cord on himself, crooked, so he'd know it from the others in the dark.
Ottie went up for a lantern. Last of the four. Said he'd bring one down for my hut too. Said he'd...
He crosses the clearing to the cold hut and sets the cap on the log seat, beside the boots, the way you'd set a place at a table.
There. He'll want that when he's back. He'll want his boots.

light.text: He leans on his rake and looks across the clearing at the cold hut, the boots on the seat.
I remember the four. Ottie. Wenna Coll. Abe and Tolly Dray, that never once agreed whose rake it was. Every night I count them. Four. I set the places in my head.
I'd not miss it, would I. If I didn't know them. I'd sleep. I'd come in by daylight and not look up the stair going out.
Take the boots. That's them. That's all of them, in Ottie's boots. Take the cap too, it goes with.
Take the boots. That's them. That's all of them, in Ottie's boots.

choice.text: Hold them in the fog, Hob. For the light.
No. Keep them. They might come back.

light_given.text: He fetches the boots from the seat and carries them to the edge of the clearing, where the fog stands close as a held breath, and holds them out into it by their laces.
He holds them a long time. His lips move: four names, counted. The leather goes cold, then silver at the toes. When he gives them to you they are heavier than boots.
There. There. Don't tell me when.

light_kept.text: They might. They might. Ottie said he'd bring a lantern for my hut.

boots_back.text: He takes the boots in both black hands and doesn't ask why. He carries them back to the cold hut's seat and sets them side by side, toes to the door.

cold_hut.text: That? Nobody's. Always been nobody's. Somebody built it and went. Burners do.
He looks at it the way you'd look at a stump: something that was a tree once, that you never saw standing.
Good poles in it. I'll have them for the clamp, come winter.

others_forgotten.text: Others? Just me. Always just me, this side of the ridge. One hearth. One clamp.
I sleep, now. Did I used to not sleep?

cap_forgotten.text: He turns the cap over in his black hands and runs a thumb along the crooked cord round the band.
Somebody's. Sewed that cord on himself, whoever he was. Crooked.
I'll put it on the shelf by the salt. Somebody might come for it.

fifth.text: Ladder's stood. Ladder's stood. I can see the light at the top of it from Bram Kettle's step, if I lean.
Four went up. Ottie. Wenna Coll. Abe and Tolly Dray. I counted them up, one at a time, and I never counted one of them down. I'd know. I'd...
You know what the Lamp told you, up there, about the ladder and the fifth. It isn't yours to tell him. It's the Lamp's.
Ottie said he'd bring a lantern down for my hut. Said he'd...

choice.text: Come up the ladder with me, Hob. Ask the Lamp yourself.
Not today.

fifth_not_today.text: Not today. Not today. It's been stood a while. It'll stand.

fifth_going.text: He looks down at the rake across his knees as if he's not sure whose it is, and leans it against the step.
Up. Up. I know the lanterns. I'll go on ahead; you're quicker than me, you'll catch me on the ladder.
Pell is across the yard before he's on his feet, holding something out in both hands: an ash-wood stick on a thong, the last notch half cut.
You're going UP? Take your stick. Finders keep FOR. You'll want to know what you were counting, now.
Hob takes it, turns it over, and puts his black thumb in the half notch.
Keep for. Keep for. Good kid.
He goes off up the cart road toward the brambles at an old man's walk, and doesn't look back, and the canes lift for him.

ridge_word.text: Hob stands at the ladder's head with the lantern held out in front of him by its bail, the way you'd hold a thing you'd been handed and weren't sure was yours. He is looking north-east, up the spine, where the old road goes on past the bare marks into the fog.
Five. I'm the fifth. You came up the lanterns. You stood the ladder. You say.

choice.text: Go after them, Hob. You've the light they went looking for.
Stay. Somebody should be at the bottom of the road when they come down.
It's yours to choose, Hob. Not mine.

ridge_go.text: After them. After them. Ottie'll want his boots.
No. No. I'll tell him where they are. He can come down for them himself. Do him good.

ridge_choose.text: Mine. Mine. Nobody's said that to me since...
He looks down the ladder at the woods, with the camp somewhere under them; then up the spine; then at the lantern in his fist.
They didn't wait to be told. Not one of them. Ottie never waited to be told a thing in his life.

ridge_walk.text: He doesn't take his leave of anybody. He sets off north-east up the spine at an old man's walk with the lantern swinging, and the heather closes behind him.
At the first bare mark he stops, takes out the count-stick and his knife, and cuts a whole notch after the one he finished. Five. Then he goes on.
I'll hang one on the second mark. So he'll see it, if he looks back. So he'll know the road down.

ridge_stay.text: Bottom of the road. Bottom of the road. That's a place, that is.
Somebody ought to know their faces, coming down. Bram Kettle won't. Bram Kettle doesn't know mine.
Then there's two of us. One at each end. That's better than one.
Hob goes back down the ladder with the lantern hooked over his arm, careful on every rung, talking to it.

shore.text: Hob stands by the colliers' fire with his lantern held out in front of him, and his lips move. One, two, three. Four. He starts again.
Four. All four, on a beach. Had them in my head every night, and here they are with their feet wet.
Three, on a beach, with their feet wet. And Ottie home, they say, to his boots. That's four. That's four.
Wenna won't go up. Wenna's waiting for a boat. I'll wait with Wenna. I'm good at it. I'm the best there is.
Counting them morning and night. Morning and night. Somebody's to.

choice.text: Goodbye, Hob.

home_from_shore.text: Hob Marl stands by his own clamp in the clearing, his lantern held out in front of him, though it's daylight and the clearing never needed one.
Came up the steps behind them. Counted them up every step. Four. Four, and me. Then I stopped. Stopped counting, top of the steps.
Ottie brought a lantern for my hut, as well. Said he'd promised. He had. I'd forgotten. He hadn't.
My rake's at Bram Kettle's, on his bench. He can keep it. Doesn't know whose it is, does he. Nobody down there does.

choice.text: Goodbye, Hob.
